title: Hard exam 3
about: Ten single-choice questions with traps: subshells, startup files, operator precedence in `find`, directories that decide who may delete, a delimiter with a space and patterns that match nothing.

questions.title: Inside the parentheses
questions.text:
A shell has `PWD=/tmp` and runs:
```
x=1
( x=2; cd /; echo "$x $PWD" )
echo "$x $PWD"
```
What does it print?

options.why: The parentheses start a subshell: its changes do not reach the parent shell.
Inside the subshell `x` is 2 and the directory is `/`.
The variable is not changed in the parent either.
The subshell sees its own values; afterwards the parent still has `x=1` and `/tmp`.

questions.title: Where a variable lives
questions.text: You append `export P=1` to your `~/.bashrc`, and nothing else. Which command prints `1`?

options.t: `echo $P` in the terminal that was already open, right now.
options.why: That shell read `.bashrc` when it started, before the edit.

options.t: `bash -c 'echo $P'` run in the terminal that was already open.
options.why: The child inherits only what the open shell exported, and it never got `P`.

options.t: `echo $P` in a new terminal opened by another user.
options.why: Each user reads their own `~/.bashrc`; this one belongs to you.

options.t: `echo $P` in a new terminal that you open yourself.
options.why: A new interactive bash reads your `~/.bashrc`, which now sets `P`.

questions.title: The right file for each setting
questions.text: `ana`, a normal user, wants an alias only for herself. The administrator, root, wants a variable defined for every user at login. Which pair of files is correct?

options.why: ana cannot write `/etc/profile`, and it would affect all users.
The personal file is in the home of the user; the one for everybody is under `/etc`.
The file in `/root` configures only the user root.
The roles are reversed: the general file is under `/etc`, and `~/.profile` is a personal one.

questions.title: A star that is only a star
questions.text: `f` contains the lines `a*b`, `aab` and `ab`. Which command prints only `a*b`?

options.why: The `*` repeats the `a`, so it matches `ab` and `aab` as well, and even `a*b` (through its final `b`).
The backslash turns the star into an ordinary character.
The dot matches any one character: it matches `a*b` and `aab`.
It matches one or more `a` followed by `b`: `aab` and `ab`.

questions.title: Who may delete
questions.text: The directory `dd` has mode `rwxrwxrwx`. Inside is `dd/f`, owned by root with mode `---------`. A normal user runs `rm -f dd/f`. What happens?

options.t: It fails with `Permission denied`, because the file has no permissions at all.
options.why: Deleting removes an entry of the directory; the file's own bits are not checked.

options.t: It fails, because the file belongs to root and only the owner can delete it.
options.why: Without the sticky bit, the permissions of the directory decide.

options.t: The file is deleted, because the user has `w` and `x` on the directory.
options.why: Removing a name needs `w` and `x` on the directory containing it.

options.t: The content of the file is emptied but the file remains.
options.why: `rm` unlinks the name; it does not truncate the file.

questions.title: Precedence in find
questions.text: In the current directory there are the files `a.log` and `b.txt`, the directory `c.txt` and the directory `dir.log`. What does `find . -name '*.log' -o -name '*.txt' -type f` print?

options.why: `-type f` applies only to the `*.txt` test, so the directory `dir.log` is also selected.
`-type f` excludes the directory `c.txt`, which would be a `*.txt` match.
The tests join with an implicit AND that binds tighter than `-o`: it is `*.log` OR (`*.txt` AND file).

options.t: Nothing, because `-o` needs parentheses to work.
options.why: `-o` works without them; the parentheses only change the grouping.

questions.title: The delimiter with a space
questions.text:
`h.sh` contains these four lines, the third one starting with a space:
```
cat <<EOF
hello
 EOF
echo after
```
What happens when it runs?

options.t: It prints `hello` and then `after`, as if the delimiter had been written correctly.
options.why: The delimiter must appear alone at the start of the line; with a space it is not recognised.

options.t: It prints `hello`, then `EOF`, and then `after` on its own line, as separate commands.
options.why: Those lines are still part of the text of the here-document, not commands.

options.t: It is not closed: bash warns about end-of-file, and `cat` prints `hello`, ` EOF` and `echo after`.
options.why: The text continues to the end of the file, because ` EOF` is not the delimiter.

options.t: A syntax error stops the script before anything at all can be printed.
options.why: Bash reads to the end of the file and only emits a warning.

questions.title: Free space and used space
questions.text: You want to know how much free space the partition mounted on `/backup` has, and how much the directory `/backup/2024` takes. Which pair of commands does that?

options.t: `du -sh /backup` for the free space and `df -h /backup/2024` for the size of the directory.
options.why: `du` measures what files use, not what is free; `df` reports whole filesystems, not directories.

options.t: `ls -l /backup` for the free space and `ls -lh /backup/2024` for the size of the directory.
options.why: `ls` shows the size of each entry, not the free space or the total of a directory tree.

options.t: `df -h /backup` for the free space and `du -sh /backup/2024` for the size of the directory.
options.why: `df` reports free and used space of the filesystem; `du -s` adds up the files below a directory.

options.t: `df -h /backup/2024` for both, because it reports the directory and its partition.
options.why: `df` gives the figures of the whole filesystem; it cannot tell how much that one directory occupies.

questions.title: The biggest files
questions.text: Which pipeline prints the five largest files of the directory, using the size in the fifth column of `ls -l`?

options.why: `-n` compares the beginning of each line, which is the mode string, not the size.
It sorts by size, but in ascending order, so these are the smallest.
It sorts only the first five lines of the listing; the order of the biggest ones is lost.
Sort by the fifth field, numerically and in reverse, then keep the first five.

questions.title: Splitting the list
questions.text:
The directory has two files, `b.txt` and `my file.txt` (the second has a space in its name). What do these two loops print?
```
n=0; for f in $(ls *.txt); do n=$((n+1)); done; echo $n
n=0; for f in *.txt; do n=$((n+1)); done; echo $n
```

options.why: The first loop gets the output of `ls` as plain text, and the shell splits it at the space.
In the second loop the pattern expands to two names, and a name with a space stays as one word.
It is the other way round: the second loop is the safe one.
`$(ls *.txt)` is split at blanks into `b.txt`, `my` and `file.txt`; the glob in the second loop gives exactly the two real names.
